Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a serious fungal disease affecting Malus species worldwide. It primarily attacks leaves and fruit, causing severe defoliation and fruit blemishes that render crops unmarketable.
symptoms: Velvety olive-green to dark brown circular spots on leaf surfaces
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and turn yellow before premature drop
Fruit develops scabby, corky, dark lesions that crack as fruit expands
Twig lesions can occur on young succulent water sprouts
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Prima, or Enterprise
Prune canopy trees annually to promote rapid drying of foliage
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to disrupt the overwintering fungal lifecycle
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that keeps leaves wet for prolonged periods
management: Apply protective fungicides (captan, sulfur, or copper compounds) at green tip through petal fall
Use weather-based disease forecasting models to time preventative sprays before rain events
Apply flail mowing of fallen leaves coupled with dilute urea spray in late autumn to accelerate leaf decomposition

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot causes leaf spot ('frog-eye' leaf spot), fruit rot, and limb cankers on apple trees, substantially lowering fruit quality and tree vigor.
symptoms: Small purple flecks on leaves expanding into circular spots with light tan centers and purple margins (frog-eye spot)
Firm, brown fruit rot with concentric rings expanding rapidly
Shriveled, mummified black fruit remaining attached to branches
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on twigs, branches, and trunks
prevention: Prune out dead wood, cankers, and mummified fruits during winter dormancy
Maintain tree vigor through balanced fertilization and soil drainage
Prevent mechanical and insect injury to bark and fruit
Burn or deeply bury all pruned diseased wood away from the orchard
management: Apply broad-spectrum fungicides from tight cluster stage through harvest
Remove newly spotted fruit immediately during the growing season
Ensure proper air circulation through regular structural pruning

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust requires two host species to complete its lifecycle: apples (Malus) and eastern red cedar or juniper (Juniperus). It leads to severe foliar discoloration and premature leaf loss.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on the upper leaf surface in spring
Raised orange blisters that exude drops of orange-brown liquid
Small tube-like fruiting structures (aecia) forming on the leaf underside
Blemished, distorted fruit near the calyx end
prevention: Eradicate nearby red cedar and juniper trees within a 1-2 mile radius of orchards if feasible
Select resistant apple varieties (e.g., Redfree, William's Pride, Freedom)
Prune galls from ornamental junipers before early spring rains
Space trees adequately to maximize wind aeration
management: Apply targeted fungicides (myclobutanil, mancozeb) starting from pink bud until petal fall
Monitor weather conditions for warm wet spring periods when cedar galls release basidiospores
Apply foliar protective sprays according to regional extension advisory schedules

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays optimal physiological health with no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, viral, or abiotic stress.
symptoms: Uniform deep green leaf color
Smooth, intact leaf margins and surfaces without lesions or chlorosis
Normal turgidity and balanced vegetative shoot growth
prevention: Continue integrated pest management (IPM) monitoring protocols
Provide regular soil moisture without waterlogging
Maintain annual pruning and balanced nitrogen-potassium nutrition
Apply dormant oil sprays in winter to control overwintering scale and mite pests
management: Routine scouting for early symptom detection
Maintain mulch layer to preserve root zone moisture and regulate soil temperature

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant displays healthy foliage with vibrant green color and absence of rust, leaf spot, or blight symptoms.
symptoms: Glossy, firm, elliptical green leaves
Unblemished leaf blades without necrotic spots or marginal burns
Vigorous shoot growth indicating appropriate acidic soil conditions
prevention: Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur
Ensure consistent drip irrigation and acidic pine bark mulch
Prune out older canes periodically to stimulate productive new canes
management: Regular soil testing for micronutrient availability (iron, zinc)
Routine IPM field monitoring

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew attacks young expanding leaves, shoots, and fruit of both sweet and tart cherries, causing curled foliage and reduced photosynthesis.
symptoms: White powdery, felt-like fungal patches on the underside or surface of leaves
Young leaves curl upwards, blister, and become brittle or distorted
Stunted shoot terminals covered with dense white mycelial growth
Infected fruit may develop sunken, white powdery lesions
prevention: Prune to promote sunlight penetration and continuous air movement through the tree canopy
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization which promotes excessive succulent shoot growth
Use under-canopy micro-sprinklers instead of overhead irrigation
management: Apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oils, or sulfur fungicides at first symptom appearance
Rotate fungicide chemical classes to prevent pathogen resistance development
Prune infected terminal shoots in early spring to suppress primary inoculum

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry foliage exhibits healthy leaf development, consistent dark green chlorophyll distribution, and no pathogen symptoms.
symptoms: Intact ovate leaves with finely serrated margins
Vibrant green coloration with no mottling, spots, or powdery growth
Healthy petiole attachment and vigorous branch structure
prevention: Maintain orchard cleanliness and prune during dry weather to prevent bacterial canker
Monitor for cherry fruit fly and aphids with yellow sticky traps
Ensure balanced soil nutrition based on periodic leaf tissue analysis
management: Maintain routine preventative orchard care
Regular soil hydration during dry summer spells

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a major foliar pathogen of maize worldwide that causes extensive photosynthetic tissue necrosis, leading to stalk lodging and yield decline.
symptoms: Small, rectangular tan-to-gray lesions running parallel between leaf veins
Lesion boundaries strictly delimited by major leaf veins
Lesions coalesce under warm humid conditions to blight large areas of the leaf
Severe premature senescence of canopy leaves during grain fill
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with documented resistance to Cercospora zeae-maydis
Implement minimum two-year crop rotation with non-host crops like soybeans
Till or bury crop residue where soil conservation practices permit
management: Scout lower leaves before tasseling (VT) stage
Apply foliar fungicides (strobilurin and triazole mixtures) if lesions reach the ear leaf at VT to R1 stage
Promote adequate plant spacing to facilitate rapid canopy drying

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is driven by cool, humid conditions and airborne fungal spores, forming reddish-brown pustules on corn leaves.
symptoms: Circular to elongate golden-brown to cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery rust-colored urediniospores
Severe infections lead to chlorosis, necrosis, and premature leaf drop
Brown pustules turn brownish-black late in the season as teliospores form
prevention: Plant corn hybrids containing specific Rp gene resistance or high general tolerance
Early planting to avoid high mid-summer spore loads blown in on prevailing winds
Maintain balanced soil fertility, avoiding excessive nitrogen
management: Apply foliar fungicides when rust pustules cover more than 5% of leaf area on upper canopy before silking
Follow regional extension rust tracking maps to anticipate spore flights

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern Corn Leaf Blight produces large cigar-shaped lesions on maize leaves, severely reducing photosynthate availability during grain development.
symptoms: Characteristic long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (1 to 6 inches long)
Lesions not restricted by leaf veins unlike gray leaf spot
Dark olive-green fuzzy spore growth on lesions during humid mornings
Entire leaves may dry out and appear prematurely killed by frost
prevention: Plant resistant maize hybrids carrying Ht resistance genes
Rotate with non-grass crops for at least one full growing season
Incorporate previous crop residue to accelerate microbial decomposition of fungal structures
management: Apply preventative fungicides at the onset of tassel emergence if lesions are present on lower third of plants
Monitor field thresholds regularly following extended periods of moderate temperatures and heavy dews

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Corn leaves display excellent vigor, unbroken parallel venation, and absence of pustules, blights, or insect feeding scars.
symptoms: Long arching leaves with consistent rich green color
Intact parallel veins and smooth leaf blade surfaces
Stout stalks and uniform collar emergence
prevention: Maintain appropriate seeding density and planting depth
Soil test regularly for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and zinc
Implement weed control during critical early growth stages (V1 to V6)
management: Continue routine scouting through grain filling stages
Ensure adequate irrigation during pollination and kernel development

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is an economically devastating disease of cultivated grapevines in warm, humid regions, attacking all green tissues and shriveling fruit into hard black mummies.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with dark borders
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) arranged in a ring inside older leaf lesions
Infected berries turn pale, soften, turn purple, and shrivel into hard black mummies
Black sunken cankers on shoots and tendrils
prevention: Prune and destroy all mummified berries from vines and ground during winter
Choose trellis designs and shoot positioning that promote sunlight and airflow
Prune suckers and manage canopy density diligently
management: Apply protective fungicides (mancozeb, captan, or myclobutanil) starting at early shoot growth (1-3 inches) through 4 weeks post-bloom
Remove shoot strikes and infected clusters promptly

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a destructive vascular wood-decay disease complex of grapevines causing distinctive tiger-stripe foliar patterns and spotty fruit rot.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' foliar symptoms with interveinal chlorosis and necrosis bounded by yellow/red bands
Small dark purple or black spots ('measles') on the skin of maturing berries
Cracking and shriveling of affected grape berries
Sudden apoplexy (complete vine collapse) during hot dry spells
prevention: Use certified disease-free rootstocks and scion wood
Apply pruning wound sealants (boron paste, paints with fungicides) immediately after pruning
Prune during late winter or dry periods when fungal spore release is lowest
Avoid large pruning wounds where possible
management: Remedial trunk surgery or vine renewal from healthy basal suckers
Mark symptomatic vines for targeted management or replacement

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Isariopsis leaf spot causes late-season blighting of grape leaves, leading to early defoliation and compromised berry ripening.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown to black necrotic spots with halos on older foliage
Dark velvety fungal sporulation on the underside of spots
Leaf tissue between spots becomes chlorotic and dies
Premature autumn defoliation weakening cold hardiness
prevention: Canopy management to ensure good ventilation and rapid leaf drying
Plow or destroy fallen leaves that harbor the overwintering teleomorph
Maintain balanced vine nutrition to prevent premature leaf stress
management: Apply copper-based fungicides or mancozeb when initial spots are identified
Ensure post-harvest spray applications if foliar disease pressure remains high

Grape___healthy.description: The grapevine foliage exhibits healthy palmate green leaves, uniform chlorophyll distribution, and no pathogen infection.
symptoms: Smooth, fully expanded palmate leaves with sharp teeth
Uniform vibrant green color with no interveinal mottling or necrotic lesions
Healthy tendril production and strong cane internode development
prevention: Maintain active canopy shoot positioning and tucking
Manage vineyard floor cover crops for balanced water and nutrient competition
Scout routinely for phylloxera, powdery mildew, and berry moths
management: Continue standard vineyard IPM protocols
Ensure drip irrigation matches vine evapotranspiration requirements

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot causes water-soaked angular leaf lesions, shot-hole symptoms, and pitted fruit cracking on stone fruit trees.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown to black
Centres of spots dry up and fall out, giving leaves a 'shot-hole' appearance
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, causing severe defoliation
Fruit develops pitted, cracked, corky lesions that exude gum
prevention: Plant resistant peach varieties (e.g., Redhaven, Candor, Biscoe)
Establish windbreaks to reduce windblown sand abrasions that introduce bacteria
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization that stimulates prolonged succulent shoot growth
management: Apply protective copper sprays at dormant and bud-swell stages
Use oxytetracycline sprays during bloom and petal fall where registered and recommended
Prune spring cankers during routine dormant pruning

Peach___healthy.description: The peach foliage shows healthy, lanceolate leaves with glossy green lamina and no bacterial or fungal spotting.
symptoms: Sleek, lanceolate leaves with serrate edges and healthy green pigmentation
Absence of chlorotic yellowing, shot-holes, or leaf curling
Vigorous extension shoots and healthy flower/fruit development
prevention: Maintain open center vase pruning architecture for adequate sunlight penetration
Apply winter dormant copper sprays to prevent peach leaf curl
Monitor soil moisture and maintain mulch rings around root zone
management: Routine orchard scouting
Timely thin fruit clusters to improve individual fruit size and tree stamina

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on bell pepper causes water-soaked lesions that brown and cause severe defoliation, leaving fruit vulnerable to sunscald.
symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on lower leaf surfaces
Lesions turn dark brown with pale centers and yellow halos
Severe leaf yellowing and heavy defoliation
Raised blister-like, rough, warty spots on fruit surfaces
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated pepper seeds
Select resistant pepper cultivars with specific Xanthomonas resistance genes
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least 2 to 3 years
Use drip irrigation to prevent water splashing
management: Apply fixed copper fungicides combined with mancozeb upon detection
Apply actigard (acibenzolar-S-methyl) for systemic acquired resistance induction
Destroy and plow under all crop residue promptly after final harvest

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper foliage exhibits smooth, dark green, healthy leaves free of bacterial flecks or viral mosaic mottling.
symptoms: Glossy, lanceolate to ovate deep green leaves
Smooth margins and absence of water-soaked lesions or puckering
Sturdy stems with healthy blossoms and expanding bell-shaped fruit
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture to prevent blossom-end rot
Employ plastic mulch and drip lines for weed and soil splash control
Ensure balanced calcium and potassium fertilization
management: Maintain routine monitoring for aphids, thrips, and mites
Keep field borders free of solanaceous weeds

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common foliar disease of potatoes that attacks older leaves first, producing characteristic concentric target-board lesions.
symptoms: Circular to angular dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding expanding lesions
Older lower foliage affected first, progressing upward as the plant matures
Severe premature defoliation reducing tuber size and total yield
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Rotate fields with non-solanaceous crops for 3 to 4 years
Maintain optimal nitrogen and potassium levels to prevent plant stress
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation late in the afternoon
management: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting when the canopy closes
Rotate with targeted systemic fungicides (succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors / QoI) to avoid resistance
Allow vines to desiccate completely before harvesting to prevent tuber infection

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is the devastating pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. Under cool, wet conditions, it can destroy an entire potato crop in days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale to dark green irregular lesions rapidly turning brown to purplish-black
Pale chlorotic halo bordering dark lesions
White fungal-like fuzzy growth (sporangia) on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Foul-smelling rotten foliage and dry granular brown rot in potato tubers
prevention: Plant certified resistant or disease-free seed tubers
Eliminate cull potato piles and volunteer potatoes near fields
Use late blight forecasting systems (e.g., BlightCast) to schedule preventative applications
Ensure hills are well-covered with soil to protect expanding tubers from washed-down spores
management: Apply protective fungicides (mandipropamid, cymoxanil, fluopicolide, chlorothalonil) before infection events
Destroy infected crop patches immediately to stop secondary spore production
Kill vines chemically or mechanically at least 2 weeks before harvest

Potato___healthy.description: The potato foliage exhibits dense, vigorous dark green compound leaves with no foliar lesions, wilting, or yellowing.
symptoms: Well-formed compound pinnate leaves with vibrant green coloration
Absence of target-spot lesions, water-soaked blights, or curling
Stout stems and vigorous stolon and tuber development
prevention: Maintain adequate hilling to protect underground tubers from sunlight and greening
Ensure balanced irrigation with tensiometer monitoring to avoid drought stress
Scout for Colorado potato beetle and potato leafhopper
management: Routine crop monitoring
Maintain sanitization protocols for tractors and implements

Rice___Bacterial_Blight.description: Bacterial blight is one of the most destructive diseases of rice in Asia and Africa, producing severe leaf blighting, kresek (seedling wilt), and unfilled grains.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes along leaf margins expanding into undulating yellow-to-white lesions
Lesions turn grayish-white as tissues die and desiccate
Milky bacterial exudate beads visible on young lesions early in the morning
Seedling 'kresek' symptom causing total wilting and death of young tillers
prevention: Grow resistant rice varieties carrying Xa resistance genes
Avoid excessive nitrogen application; apply nitrogen in split doses
Ensure good field drainage during heavy monsoon periods
Clean irrigation canals and eliminate weed hosts like Leersia hexandra
management: Apply copper hydroxide or validated bactericide sprays where permitted
Drain standing water temporarily to slow bacterial spread across paddies
Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips before transplanting

Rice___Brown_Spot.description: Rice brown spot is a foliar fungal disease historically associated with the Great Bengal Famine of 1943. It predominantly targets nutrient-deficient or moisture-stressed rice crops.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval sesame-seed shaped brown spots with gray or whitish centers
Yellow halo surrounding mature spots
Lesions coalesce to cover entire leaf surfaces causing premature blighting
Infected panicle glumes develop dark brown discolorations, reducing grain quality
prevention: Treat seeds with hot water (52-54 deg C for 15 min) or certified seed fungicides
Correct soil nutrient deficiencies, especially potassium, silicon, and zinc
Maintain proper field water levels to avoid intermittent drought stress
management: Apply foliar fungicides (edifenphos, mancozeb, or triazoles) at tillering and boot leaf emergence
Apply balanced potassium top-dressing to bolster plant epidermal cell walls

Rice___Leaf_Smut.description: Rice leaf smut produces small angular black spots on rice leaves, occurring mostly on mature plants toward late reproductive stages.
symptoms: Small, slightly raised, angular black spots on both sides of the leaf blade
Spots remain distinct and do not coalesce like brown spot
In heavy infections, leaves turn yellow from the tip downward and die early
Epidermis covering spots ruptures during humid weather to release black powdery teliospores
prevention: Maintain balanced plant nutrition, avoiding excessive nitrogen fertilizer
Use certified disease-free seeds
Burn or plow under rice stubble after harvest to eliminate overwintering teliospores
management: Apply protectant copper or sulfur foliar sprays if disease appears before heading
Ensure proper irrigation and field drainage

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch affects the foliage, petioles, runners, and fruit calyx of strawberry plants, causing leaves to look dried, scorched, and burned.
symptoms: Numerous irregular small purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots expand and coalesce, turning the entire leaf purplish-brown
Leaf edges curl upward and leaves appear scorched and dead
Infected fruit calyxes turn brown and dry up, reducing fruit attractiveness
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry plugs or bare-root plants
Select resistant varieties (e.g., Honeoye, Allstar, Cavendish)
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing old foliage and removing debris
Use drip irrigation under plastic mulch to keep foliage completely dry
management: Apply protective fungicides (captan, dodine, or thiophanate-methyl) early in the spring
Remove severely scorched leaves during spring sanitation
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen in spring

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry foliage displays healthy trifoliate leaves, rich emerald color, and no fungal spots or scorch markings.
symptoms: Vibrant green, serrated trifoliate leaves with healthy turgidity
Absence of purple flecks, necrosis, or edge curling
Healthy runner formation and abundant white blossoms
prevention: Maintain straw or plastic mulch to keep fruit and leaves off bare soil
Ensure steady soil moisture with drip lines
Scout for two-spotted spider mites and tarnished plant bugs
management: Routine crop monitoring
Remove old senescing leaves periodically to encourage new crown growth

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot causes water-soaked angular leaf spots, defoliation, and unsightly fruit lesions on field and greenhouse tomatoes.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked circular to angular lesions on leaves
Lesions develop a greasy appearance and often have a narrow yellow halo
Centers of lesions dry up and tear easily
Fruit develops raised, scabby, rough dark spots with light margins
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water treated seed (50 deg C for 25 min)
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 years
Sanitize stakes, cages, and greenhouse equipment
Avoid working in tomato fields when leaves are wet
management: Apply copper bactericides combined with mancozeb upon initial detection
Apply bacteriophage products or systemic resistance activators where available
Incorporate crop residues deeply into the soil immediately after harvest

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a very common destructive fungal disease of tomatoes, attacking foliage, stems, and fruit throughout the growing season.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with distinct concentric rings ('target-board' appearance)
Yellow chlorotic tissue surrounding expanding lesions
Bottom-up defoliation exposing fruit to sunscald
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at the stem end of tomato fruit
prevention: Stake or cage plants and prune lower sucker branches to keep leaves off the ground
Mulch soil around plants with straw or plastic to prevent splash dispersal
Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers
management: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper fungicides, or azoxystrobin) at first sign
Prune and dispose of infected lower leaves immediately
Clear all plant residue thoroughly in the fall

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is an aggressive water mold pathogen that causes rapid collapse and rotting of tomato leaves, stems, and green fruit during cool wet weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked lesions that turn dark brown to purplish-black
Delicate white cottony mold on the undersides of infected leaves during moist mornings
Stems develop dark greasy brown lesions that cause plant collapse
Fruit develops large, firm, greasy brown lesions that rot quickly
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Plum Regal)
Eliminate volunteer tomatoes and nearby potato cull piles
Maximize row spacing and airflow
Monitor regional late blight tracking maps (e.g., USAblight)
management: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper) before cool rain events
Apply systemic oomycide fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid) upon local confirmation
Bag and remove infected plants immediately to prevent spore dispersal to neighboring fields

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold primarily affects tomatoes grown in high tunnels, greenhouses, and humid environments, causing extensive yellowing and defoliation.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish patches on upper leaf surfaces with indistinct margins
Dense, olive-green to velvety brown mold growth on the corresponding lower surface
Leaves curl, wither, turn brown, and drop prematurely
Blossoms and fruit occasionally attacked, causing flower drop
prevention: Maintain relative humidity below 85% in greenhouses via heating and active ventilation
Space plants generously to promote airflow through the canopy
Plant leaf mold-resistant greenhouse cultivars (carrying Cf resistance genes)
Water exclusively via drip irrigation
management: Apply approved fungicides (copper, chlorothalonil, or biofungicides) at first sign
Prune lower foliage systematically to improve air drainage

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is one of the most destructive foliar diseases of tomatoes in humid climates, producing hundreds of tiny spots that cause progressive defoliation.
symptoms: Numerous small (1/16 to 1/8 inch), circular spots with dark brown margins and gray/tan centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible inside the center of mature spots
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop
Defoliation starts from the bottom leaves upward, exposing fruit to sunscald
prevention: Mulch soil around plants immediately after transplanting
Practice 2 to 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base of plants early in the day
Prune bottom 12 inches of foliage after plants are established
management: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, copper, or mancozeb) every 7-10 days in wet seasons
Remove and destroy infected leaves during dry weather
Till or deep-plow crop debris after harvest

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnid pests that pierce plant cell walls and suck out sap, causing stippling, bronzing, and webbing in hot dry conditions.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (tiny dots) on the upper leaf surface
Leaves turn yellow, bronze, dry out, and drop prematurely
Fine silky webbing on the undersides of leaves and along growing tips
Microscopic yellow-green mites with two dark spots visible under 10x magnification
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which creates nutrient-rich foliage for mite reproduction
Keep field borders and greenhouse entrances free of weeds
Maintain adequate irrigation; drought-stressed plants are much more susceptible
Wash dust off foliage on field borders
management: Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus) early in the season
Apply insecticidal soaps, neem oil, or horticultural oils ensuring complete coverage of leaf undersides
Rotate miticide chemical modes of action to prevent rapid resistance buildup

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot causes brown circular lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit that can rapidly cause severe canopy blight in warm humid conditions.
symptoms: Brown circular lesions with faint concentric rings and light brown centers
Lesions surrounded by a narrow yellow halo
Extensive leaf yellowing and blighting as lesions expand and coalesce
Fruit develops small, slightly sunken circular lesions that expand and crack
prevention: Ensure wide plant spacing for optimum canopy ventilation
Avoid working in damp crops to prevent mechanical spread
Rotate with non-host crops like corn or sorghum
Use drip irrigation under mulch
management: Apply protective and systemic fungicides (chlorothalonil, fluopyram, or azoxystrobin) according to label instructions
Remove infected leaves from the lower canopy promptly

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus is a devastating viral disease transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), resulting in severe plant stunting and total yield loss.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaf margins
Pronounced interveinal and marginal yellowing (chlorosis)
Leaves are significantly reduced in size and have a puckered, leathery texture
Severe plant stunting with an erect, bushy appearance and failure to set fruit
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids (carrying Ty-1 or Ty-3 resistance genes)
Install fine insect-proof mesh netting (50-mesh) on greenhouse vents
Use reflective silver mulches to repel whitefly vectors
Eradicate infected plants immediately upon symptom appearance to reduce viral reservoir
management: Target whitefly populations with insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or systemic insecticides
Maintain strict weed host control around fields
Observe a crop-free period between tomato growing cycles

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus is an extremely stable and infectious virus that causes mottled leaves, distorted foliage, and poor fruit yield. It is easily spread by mechanical contact.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottling (mosaic pattern) on leaves
Leaf distortion, blistering, and 'shoestring' narrowing of leaflets
Stunted overall plant growth
Fruit develops internal brown browning and uneven ripening
prevention: Plant resistant tomato cultivars with Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance genes
Workers should wash hands with soap and water or skim milk before handling plants
Do not use tobacco products near tomato plants
Disinfect all pruning tools with a 20% nonfat dry milk solution or 10% bleach
management: No chemical cure exists for viral infections; rogue and destroy infected plants immediately
Avoid handling healthy plants after touching suspect plants

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato foliage displays optimal physiological health with deep green compound leaves, active photosynthesis, and absence of lesions, mottling, or curling.
symptoms: Vibrant green compound leaves with healthy leaf turgor
Clean leaf blades without spots, halos, or powdery growth
Sturdy main stem and branches with active blossoming and fruit set
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture through automated drip irrigation
Prune lower suckers and provide sturdy staking or trellis support
Apply balanced tomato fertilizer with adequate calcium to prevent blossom-end rot
Scout regularly for early pest and disease pressure
management: Continue standard IPM protocols
Ensure good weed management and air circulation around plants
